patient.name: Charlotte Bennett
patient.complaint: Exhausted for 8 months since glandular fever; 'wiped out' for days after any effort
background: Secondary school teacher in Greenwich; now on reduced hours
Previously ran 10 km three times a week
No regular medicines; no low mood before this illness

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with months of disabling fatigue after a viral illness, post-exertional malaise and normal bloods. Distractors: depression, hypothyroidism, anaemia, fibromyalgia.

points: One day of marking leaves her in bed for **two days**.
Sleeps 10 hours but wakes unrefreshed; loses words mid-sentence.

steps.lead: Charlotte's fatigue is severe, persistent and **disabling**, and gets worse after effort: the definition of CFS.
Her illness started after a **viral infection** (EBV), the classic trigger.

visual.title: How long has Charlotte had symptoms?
visual.label: Charlotte 8 months
visual.caption: Adults need symptoms for at least 3 months.

points: Aching muscles and joints, but no joint swelling.
Headaches, sore throat and tender neck glands on and off.
Dizzy if she stands for long in assembly.
Enjoys her family; mood 'frustrated, not depressed'.

steps.lead: Charlotte ticks all four NICE criteria for over 3 months, plus myalgia, arthralgia without inflammation, sore throat and orthostatic dizziness.

visual.title: Charlotte's symptoms after a busy school day
visual.caption: The crash comes a day or two later and lasts days: post-exertional malaise.

steps.lead: Two days in bed after one day of marking is **post-exertional malaise**: the hallmark that separates CFS from ordinary tiredness.

steps.q: Charlotte is now off work 2 days a week and has stopped seeing friends. What is this?
steps.r: Loss of work and **social isolation** are recognised complications of CFS.

steps.lead: Charlotte is already losing work time and contact with friends; deconditioning and low mood can follow.

steps.text: Coexisting anxiety or low mood does **not** exclude CFS. Ask what is driving the fatigue: effort (CFS) or mood (depression).

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (a baseline blood panel to exclude mimics) and that CFS is a clinical diagnosis with routine tests typically normal.

steps.q: Which test confirms that Charlotte has CFS?
o: No test: it is a clinical diagnosis
steps.r: There is **no confirmatory test**. CFS is diagnosed clinically after excluding other causes.

steps.lead: No scan or blood test proves Charlotte has CFS; the diagnosis rests on her history after mimics are excluded.
Charlotte's clinical assessment looks for other causes, and her 8 months is well beyond the **3-month** minimum.

points: Examination: looks tired; mild tenderness over shoulder muscles.
No lymphadenopathy, no joint swelling, no pallor.
Pulse rises from 78 to 104 bpm on standing for 5 minutes.

steps.lead: Charlotte's exam is essentially normal apart from **orthostatic** symptoms and non-specific tenderness, as expected.

steps.title: Charlotte's baseline bloods
steps.text: All normal. That is the expected result in CFS: the tests exclude mimics.

steps.lead: Charlotte's bloods rule out **anaemia, hypothyroidism, diabetes and inflammatory disease**.

visual.title: Charlotte's ferritin
visual.label: Charlotte 64
visual.caption: Normal ferritin: iron deficiency is not the cause of her fatigue.

steps.text: In CFS questions, the 'most likely result' of routine bloods is **all within normal limits**.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate management?': energy management (pacing). Also low-dose amitriptyline for sleep or pain, CBT as support, and urgent review if severely affected.

steps.q: Charlotte asks: 'What do I do first?' What is the main first-line strategy?
steps.r: After **confirming and validating** the diagnosis, the core strategy is **pacing**: staying within her energy limits.

steps.lead: Charlotte is told clearly that her illness is real. She then learns to **pace**: balancing activity and rest to avoid crashes.

visual.title: Boom-bust vs pacing (Charlotte's activity diary)
visual.caption: Steady activity inside her limits avoids the crashes.

steps.text: Do not choose **graded exercise therapy** or 'push through it'. Current NICE guidance advises against it; overexertion causes relapse.

steps.lead: Charlotte is offered **CBT** to help her cope and support rehabilitation, framed as support, not a cure. Her headaches are treated directly.

points: Three months on: crashes are rarer, but sleep is poor.
GP starts **amitriptyline 10 mg** at night, increased slowly.
School agrees a phased return with a lighter timetable.

steps.lead: Low-dose **amitriptyline** helps Charlotte's sleep and pain. Workplace adjustments and regular review support her function.

steps.title: Charlotte's management
nodes: CBT and treat sleep, pain, headache

steps.lead: Charlotte is managing at home. If she could not eat, drink or care for herself, she would need **urgent review**.
The NICE ME/CFS guideline sets out Charlotte's plan: validation, pacing, symptom management and support.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: the multisystem mechanism, why it follows infection, why there is orthostatic intolerance, and the deconditioning cycle.

steps.lead: Nobody can point to one broken organ in Charlotte: CFS is a **multisystem** condition of unclear cause.
Charlotte's glandular fever is the likely trigger: an **aberrant or persistent immune response** after infection.
Charlotte's two-day crash after marking is abnormal and disproportionate; a merely unfit person would recover by the next day.

steps.q: Charlotte's pulse rose from 78 to 104 bpm on standing. Which mechanism best explains this?
steps.r: **Autonomic dysfunction** is thought to drive both orthostatic intolerance and unrefreshing sleep.

steps.lead: The same autonomic problem explains Charlotte's dizziness in assembly and her unrefreshing sleep.

steps.title: The deconditioning cycle
steps.caption: A self-reinforcing loop that pacing aims to break safely.

steps.lead: Charlotte's months of reduced activity are making her less fit, which feeds the fatigue: a **self-reinforcing cycle**.

mcq.q: How long must symptoms be present before diagnosing CFS in an adult?
What is the hallmark feature of CFS?
mcq.r: **Post-exertional malaise** separates CFS from ordinary fatigue and deconditioning.

mcq.q: What commonly precedes the onset of CFS?
Which is one of the four NICE core criteria for CFS?
mcq.r: Fatigue, post-exertional malaise, **unrefreshing sleep** and cognitive difficulty.
A **clinical diagnosis**; there is no confirmatory test.

mcq.q: What do routine blood tests usually show in CFS?
mcq.r: Routine investigations are typically **normal**; they exclude mimics.

mcq.q: What is the main non-pharmacological strategy in CFS?
mcq.r: **Pacing**: balance activity and rest within energy limits.

mcq.q: Which drug at low dose can help sleep and muscle pain in CFS?
What is thought to cause orthostatic intolerance in CFS?
mcq.r: **Autonomic dysfunction** contributes to orthostatic intolerance and unrefreshing sleep.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman has a 6 month history of severe tiredness that began after a flu-like illness. After a short walk she is exhausted for the next two days. Her sleep is unrefreshing and she struggles to find words. She enjoys seeing her friends when she has energy. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg. Examination and baseline bloods are normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis question about chronic fatigue: look for the hallmark feature.

clues: exhausted for the next two days
steps.x: Over 3 months, viral trigger, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep, brain fog, normal tests.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic fatigue syndrome.**

elim: She keeps enjoyment; low mood is not the core.
Fibromyalgia is dominated by widespread pain, not post-exertional malaise.
Bloods, including TFTs, are normal.
A normal FBC excludes anaemia.

steps.x: **A. CFS.** Rule: post-exertional malaise + over 3 months + normal tests = CFS.

technique.stem: A 24 year old man has had 5 months of disabling fatigue, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep and poor concentration after a viral illness. Examination is normal and baseline blood tests are all normal. He asks which test will prove what is wrong.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate response?
o: Cardiopulmonary exercise testing will confirm it
It is a clinical diagnosis with no confirmatory test

steps.x: Diagnostic investigation for CFS: is there a gold-standard test?

clues: baseline blood tests are all normal
steps.x: Classic CFS with mimics excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: There is **no confirmatory test**: CFS is a **clinical diagnosis** after exclusion.

elim: Exercise testing is not used to diagnose CFS.
EBV serology shows past infection, not CFS.
MRI is normal and not diagnostic.
Muscle biopsy has no role.

steps.x: **C. Clinical diagnosis.** Rule: in CFS the tests only rule things out.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome has been pacing her activity for 3 months. Her crashes are less frequent, but she feels she is not coping with the uncertainty of her illness and finds rehabilitation hard. She has no suicidal thoughts.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate additional intervention?

steps.x: Additional management: what supports coping and rehabilitation?
Pacing is in place; she needs help with coping and rehabilitation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **CBT** supports symptom management and rehabilitation; it is not a cure.

elim: There is no active infection to treat.
NICE advises against graded exercise therapy; overexertion causes relapse.
Benzodiazepines cause dependence and do not help CFS.
Prolonged rest worsens deconditioning.

steps.x: **B. CBT** as part of a supportive package.

technique.stem: A 19 year old student develops disabling fatigue, post-exertional malaise and recurrent sore throats 2 months after glandular fever. Six months later all blood tests remain normal. She asks why a virus could have caused this.
technique.q: Which is the most likely explanation?
o: Aberrant or persistent immune response after infection

steps.x: Mechanism: why does CFS follow infection?
An infective trigger with normal tests.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: An **aberrant or persistent immune/inflammatory response** in at least some cases.

elim: Thyroid tests are normal.
LFTs are normal.
Ferritin and FBC are normal.
Splenic rupture is an acute emergency, not chronic fatigue.

steps.x: **A. Aberrant or persistent immune response.**

practice.stem: A 31 year old man has had 7 months of exhausting tiredness since a viral illness. A day at work leaves him bedbound for the following two days. He wakes unrefreshed and has muscle aches and headaches. His temperature is 36.6°C, pulse rate 78 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Post-exertional malaise and unrefreshing sleep for over 3 months after a viral illness, with normal bloods, is CFS.

steps.x: Diagnosis: chronic tiredness after a virus.

clues: bedbound for the following two days
steps.x: Over 3 months, viral trigger, post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Chronic fatigue syndrome.**

elim: No low mood or anhedonia.
Bloods are normal.
OSA causes daytime sleepiness and snoring; no PEM.
PMR affects over 50s with raised ESR and girdle stiffness.

steps.x: **A. CFS.**

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman has had 5 months of severe fatigue after a chest infection. She has normal bloods. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. The GP wants to confirm the feature that best separates her illness from simple deconditioning.
practice.q: Which feature most strongly supports the likely diagnosis?
o: Symptoms worsening for days after minor exertion
practice.e: Post-exertional malaise is the hallmark of CFS and distinguishes it from ordinary fatigue or deconditioning.

steps.x: Which feature is the hallmark?

clues: separates her illness from simple deconditioning
steps.x: The question is pointing at the signature feature of CFS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Post-exertional malaise**: disproportionate worsening after minor exertion.

elim: Breathlessness on stairs fits deconditioning or heart and lung disease.
Napping is non-specific.
Weakness suggests a neuromuscular cause.
Weight gain suggests hypothyroidism.

steps.x: **D. Symptoms worsening for days after minor exertion.**

practice.stem: A 35 year old woman has had 6 months of disabling fatigue with post-exertional malaise. She asks what might have started it. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which preceding event is most commonly associated with this condition?
practice.e: CFS onset frequently follows a viral illness, and flu-like symptoms can mark the start and recur.

steps.x: Most likely trigger.
This is CFS. Its onset frequently follows an infection.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **viral illness**.

elim: Head injury is not the classic trigger.
Surgery is not the classic trigger.
Travel alone is not a recognised trigger.
The pill does not cause CFS.

steps.x: **E. Viral illness.** Flu-like symptoms often mark the start.

practice.stem: A 22 year old man has had 9 months of fatigue with post-exertional malaise, unrefreshing sleep and poor concentration after glandular fever. Baseline bloods are normal. He also reports aching knees and wrists.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of his joints?
practice.e: CFS causes arthralgia without inflammation, and examination is usually normal. Synovitis or effusions point to another diagnosis.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding in CFS arthralgia.
CFS causes generalised arthralgia **without inflammation**; examination is usually normal.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **No joint swelling or inflammation.**

elim: Heberden's nodes are osteoarthritis.
A hot effusion suggests septic or crystal arthritis.
Synovitis suggests rheumatoid arthritis.
Tophi are gout.

steps.x: **C. No joint swelling or inflammation.**

practice.stem: A 40 year old woman has had 8 months of fatigue after a viral illness, made worse for days by minor effort. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 120/78 mmHg. Bloods are normal.
practice.q: Which additional symptom is most consistent with the likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Unrefreshing sleep is a core NICE criterion for CFS. Fevers, sweats, weight loss and prolonged stiffness suggest another diagnosis.

steps.x: Which symptom fits the diagnosis?

clues: 8 months of fatigue after a viral illness
made worse for days by minor effort
steps.x: This is CFS. Unrefreshing sleep is one of the four NICE criteria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Unrefreshing sleep.**

elim: High fevers suggest infection or malignancy.
Night sweats suggest TB or lymphoma.
Prolonged morning stiffness suggests inflammatory arthritis.
Weight loss is a red flag for another cause.

steps.x: **E. Unrefreshing sleep.**

practice.stem: A 26 year old man has had chronic fatigue syndrome for 2 years. He has spent most of that time resting at home. He now becomes breathless and tired with even less activity than a year ago. His pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 116/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his falling exercise tolerance?
practice.e: Chronic disability in CFS leads to secondary deconditioning, which further reduces exercise tolerance and perpetuates the fatigue.

steps.x: Most likely cause: what does long-term inactivity do?

clues: spent most of that time resting at home
even less activity than a year ago
steps.x: Prolonged inactivity in CFS reduces fitness.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Secondary deconditioning**, which perpetuates the fatigue.

elim: Nothing suggests blood loss or pallor.
No signs of heart failure.
No features of hypothyroidism.
No cough, crackles or clubbing.

steps.x: **E. Secondary deconditioning.** A complication of CFS and a self-reinforcing cycle.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has had 4 months of disabling fatigue after a viral illness, with post-exertional malaise and unrefreshing sleep. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 118/72 mmHg. Examination is normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, CRP/ESR, glucose, B12, folate and ferritin
practice.e: Baseline bloods exclude anaemia, hypothyroidism, diabetes and inflammatory disease before CFS is diagnosed.

steps.x: Initial investigation in suspected CFS.
Probable CFS; mimics must be excluded.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: A **baseline blood panel**: FBC, U&E, LFTs, TFTs, CRP/ESR, glucose, B12, folate, ferritin.

elim: CT is for red flags such as weight loss.
EBV serology does not diagnose CFS.
No neurological signs.
No snoring or apnoeas.

steps.x: **C. The baseline blood panel.**

practice.stem: A 28 year old man has had 6 months of fatigue with post-exertional malaise, myalgia and cognitive difficulty after a viral illness. His pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg. Examination is normal apart from non-specific muscle tenderness. Baseline blood tests are sent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely result?
practice.e: Routine investigations are typically normal in CFS. An abnormal result should prompt a search for another cause.

steps.x: Most likely test result in CFS.
Classic CFS. Routine tests exclude mimics.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Routine investigations are typically **normal**.

elim: Low ferritin points to iron deficiency.
Low T4 points to hypothyroidism.
Raised CK suggests a myopathy.
Raised ESR suggests inflammatory disease.

steps.x: **A. All within normal limits.**

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman has just been diagnosed with chronic fatigue syndrome. She tends to do a lot on good days and then crashes for several days. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Pacing (energy management) balances activity and rest within energy limits to avoid relapse. Overexertion, including graded exercise, worsens symptoms.

steps.x: First-line management of CFS.

clues: do a lot on good days and then crashes
steps.x: Boom-bust activity in newly diagnosed CFS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Energy management (pacing)**, after validating the diagnosis.

elim: NICE advises against graded exercise therapy.
Steroids have no role.
Prolonged rest causes deconditioning.
Antidepressants are not first-line without depression.

steps.x: **C. Pacing.**

practice.stem: A 36 year old man with chronic fatigue syndrome is pacing well, but poor sleep and widespread muscle pain are limiting him. His pulse rate is 76 bpm and BP 124/80 mmHg. He has no low mood.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate drug?
practice.e: Low-dose tricyclics such as amitriptyline can improve sleep and musculoskeletal pain in CFS, especially combined with pacing.

steps.x: Drug for sleep and pain in CFS.

clues: poor sleep and widespread muscle pain
steps.x: CFS with sleep disturbance and musculoskeletal pain.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low-dose amitriptyline**, increased gradually.

elim: Opioids risk dependence and do not help sleep quality.
Benzodiazepines cause dependence.
There is no inflammation to treat.
Hypnotics are short-term only and do not help pain.

steps.x: **C. Low-dose amitriptyline.**

practice.stem: A 23 year old woman with severe chronic fatigue syndrome is bedbound. Her mother says she has barely eaten or drunk for 3 days and cannot wash or go to the toilet alone. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm and BP 96/60 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next step?
practice.e: Profound functional decline, dehydration or malnutrition, or inability to self-care needs urgent or emergency review.

steps.x: Emergency management: is she safe at home?

clues: barely eaten or drunk for 3 days
cannot wash or go to the toilet alone
steps.x: Dehydration, malnutrition and inability to self-care.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Urgent review**.

elim: Drug changes do not address dehydration.
Routine CBT is far too slow.
Waiting is unsafe.
Exercise is inappropriate and unsafe here.

steps.x: **A. Urgent same-day assessment.**

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman with chronic fatigue syndrome feels dizzy and faint when she stands for more than a few minutes. Her lying pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 114/72 mmHg; after 5 minutes standing her pulse rate is 106 bpm. She also has unrefreshing sleep.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms?
practice.e: Autonomic dysfunction is thought to contribute to both orthostatic intolerance and unrefreshing sleep in CFS.

steps.x: Mechanism: what links orthostatic intolerance and unrefreshing sleep in CFS?

clues: dizzy and faint when she stands
after 5 minutes standing her pulse rate is 106 bpm
steps.x: Orthostatic tachycardia plus unrefreshing sleep in CFS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Autonomic dysfunction** contributes to both.

elim: No pallor; a sinus rise on standing is postural.
A regular postural rise is not an arrhythmia.
Hypothyroidism causes bradycardia.
Vasovagal syncope gives bradycardia and hypotension, not tachycardia.

steps.x: **B. Autonomic dysfunction.**

prompts.q: What is chronic fatigue syndrome and what usually triggers it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem nearly always gives a viral illness months earlier.

points.p: Onset often follows a viral illness
points.why: Flu-like symptoms can mark the start and recur.

points.p: May coexist with anxiety or low mood
points.why: Coexisting mood symptoms do not exclude CFS.

prompts.q: What are the four NICE criteria for CFS and the duration needed in adults?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: check the duration in the stem first.

points.p: At least 3 months in adults, not explained by another condition
points.why: Too early to diagnose before 3 months.

prompts.q: What other symptoms occur in CFS, and what is the hallmark feature?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: these extras help you spot CFS among fatigue stems.

points.p: Hallmark: post-exertional malaise, distinguishing it from deconditioning
points.why: Disproportionate worsening after even minor effort.

prompts.q: What are the complications of CFS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: think function, social life and fitness.

points.p: Functional disability, loss of school or work

points.why: Can develop secondary to the illness.

points.p: Deconditioning and reduced quality of life

prompts.q: How is CFS diagnosed and which blood tests are done?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tests exclude mimics; nothing confirms CFS.

points.p: Clinical diagnosis after excluding other causes, no confirmatory test

points.why: Exclude anaemia, hypothyroidism, liver and kidney disease.
An abnormal result suggests another diagnosis.

prompts.q: What would you expect on examination in CFS?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: a normal examination is the expected finding.

prompts.q: How is CFS managed, from first-line to long-term?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: pacing first; graded exercise is the trap.

points.why: Balance activity and rest to avoid relapse.

points.p: CBT as support, not a cure
Low-dose tricyclic (amitriptyline) for sleep and pain
Work or school adjustments and regular review
Urgent review if unable to self-care, dehydrated or malnourished

prompts.q: What is the pathophysiology of CFS and why does it follow infection?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: multisystem, immune, autonomic, energy metabolism.

points.why: No single cause has been found.

points.p: Immune dysregulation; aberrant or persistent response after infection
Abnormal central and autonomic nervous system responses
points.why: Linked to orthostatic intolerance and unrefreshing sleep.

prompts.q: Why does chronic disability make the fatigue worse?

points.p: Further reduces exercise tolerance and perpetuates fatigue

points.why: Pacing aims to break it safely.

glossary.CFS: Chronic fatigue syndrome: disabling fatigue with post-exertional malaise for at least 3 months, not explained by another condition.
glossary.ME/CFS: Myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome; the name used in the NICE guideline.
glossary.chronic fatigue syndrome: Long-term disabling fatigue worsened by exertion, often after a viral illness.
glossary.post-exertional malaise: Disproportionate worsening of symptoms, often delayed, after even minor physical, mental or emotional effort.
glossary.unrefreshing sleep: Sleep that does not restore energy despite adequate hours.
glossary.brain fog: Difficulty thinking, concentrating and finding words.
glossary.orthostatic intolerance: Symptoms such as dizziness and racing heart on standing that ease on lying down.
glossary.arthralgia: Joint pain without swelling or inflammation.
glossary.deconditioning: Loss of physical fitness from prolonged inactivity.
glossary.glandular fever: Infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus; a classic trigger of CFS.
glossary.EBV: Epstein-Barr virus, the cause of glandular fever.
glossary.pacing: Energy management: balancing activity and rest to stay within energy limits and avoid crashes.
glossary.energy management: Planning activity and rest to stay within the energy available.
glossary.boom-bust: Doing too much on good days and then crashing for days afterwards.
glossary.graded exercise therapy: Fixed, increasing exercise programme; NICE now advises against it in ME/CFS.
glossary.CBT: Cognitive behavioural therapy; supports coping and rehabilitation in CFS but is not a cure.
glossary.amitriptyline: Tricyclic antidepressant used at low dose for sleep and pain.
glossary.tricyclic antidepressants: Older antidepressant class; low doses help pain and sleep.
glossary.autonomic dysfunction: Faulty control of automatic functions such as heart rate and blood pressure.
glossary.autonomic nervous system: Nerves controlling involuntary functions such as heart rate, blood pressure and sweating.
glossary.mitochondrial: Relating to mitochondria, the parts of cells that produce energy.
glossary.immune dysregulation: An immune system that responds abnormally or fails to switch off.
glossary.multisystem: Affecting several body systems at once.
glossary.ferritin: Blood marker of iron stores; low in iron deficiency.
glossary.TFTs: Thyroid function tests: TSH and free T4.
glossary.ESR: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate; a non-specific marker of inflammation.
glossary.CRP: C-reactive protein; rises with inflammation or infection.
glossary.B12: Vitamin needed for blood cells and nerves; deficiency causes tiredness and anaemia.
glossary.folate: B vitamin needed to make red cells.
glossary.hypothyroidism: Underactive thyroid, causing tiredness, weight gain and cold intolerance; a CFS mimic.
glossary.fibromyalgia: Chronic widespread pain with tender points; pain rather than PEM dominates.
